docs.flippable.component: `Flippable` is the card turn. It draws nothing — it ANSWERS one question: when the element is
turned over, which SURFACE shows? The answer is pure data, so a test reads it without a renderer
and a saved game reopens on the right side.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, Surfaced, Flippable, shownSurface } from "game-kit"
const card = node("card",
Bounded({ bounds: rect(1, 1.4) }),
Surfaced({ surface: "queen" }),
Flippable({ back: "tartan" }))
shownSurface(card, true)   // "queen"  — face-up is always the front
shownSurface(card, false)  // "tartan" — the down-side
## One field
`back` — the surface shown face-down. That is the whole atom, and it used to be four.
There was a `reverse` with `back` / `same` / `mirror` / `alt`, and it was three values pretending
to be distinct. «A separate back» and «a per-card second face» put a DIFFERENT surface on the
down-side and are the same operation. «mirror» named a reflection no painter here can draw. «same»
is just an empty back. What actually changes a pixel is one thing — the down-side surface — so
that is the one field left.
## An empty back
Leave `back` empty and the turn shows the FRONT, not nothing. A token identical on both sides needs
no back at all, and a half-configured card never turns up blank. Requiring `Surfaced` is the other
half of that promise: no face, nothing to turn, and `shownSurface` answers `undefined`.
## The side is not stored here
Which side is up is RUNTIME state — the card is turned in the course of a game — so it is passed
to `shownSurface`, never kept on the atom. `Flippable` holds only what the down-side IS, which is
spec: it does not change from turn to turn, lives on the node, and crosses the wire once.
## Why a name and not the colours
Both sides are surface NAMES, registered records. Re-register the back and every card wearing it
turns over to the new look in one step; the wire carries the short stable string, not a palette two
clients could disagree about.
docs.flippable.turn: One card and a switch that turns it. `faceUp` is the runtime side — the only thing `shownSurface`
is told beyond the node itself. Flip it and the paint changes, because the resolver chose the
other surface: there is no second code path anywhere that says «the card is face-down».
The two colours are the front and the back. Empty the back and turn the card: it does not go blank,
it shows the front — the same fallback the atom makes when no down-side surface is named.
The front here is `panelBg`, close to the table, so face-up the card is nearly invisible — that is
the point of the switch. Turn it over and the `accent` back is unmistakable.
